q: Container vs virtual machine?
short: Containers share the host OS kernel and package only app, runtime and libraries (MBs, seconds to start); VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor (GBs, minutes) with stronger isolation.

q: Dockerfile vs image vs container?
short: Dockerfile: build instructions. Image: layered, read-only template built from it. Container: a running instance; one image can run many containers.
mistakes: Editing a running container instead of the Dockerfile.

q: What goes into an ML model container?
short: Model artifact (.pkl/.onnx/.pt/.h5), inference API code, dependencies, runtime, configuration, and pre/post-processing.
follow: Model in image vs downloaded at start?

q: What does Kubernetes provide?
short: Container orchestration: scheduling across nodes, horizontal scaling/autoscaling, load balancing via services, self-healing, rolling updates, high availability and disaster recovery.
mistakes: Using it for a single small service.

q: Name the control-plane components.
short: API server (entry point, persists to etcd), etcd (key-value state store), scheduler (assigns pods to nodes), controller manager (ReplicaSet/Deployment controllers reconcile state).

q: What is a pod?
short: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network namespace and storage, with its own IP, scheduled together on one node.
mistakes: Managing pods directly instead of Deployments.

q: How do Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pod relate?
short: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets (one per version, enabling rolling updates and rollbacks); a ReplicaSet keeps the desired number of identical pods running.
follow: How does a rolling update work?

q: What is CI/CD?
short: Continuous integration automatically tests and builds every change; continuous delivery/deployment automatically releases tested artifacts to environments.
detail: For ML also data and model checks.

q: What is GitOps?
short: Using a Git repository as the single source of truth for the desired deployment state; an agent (Argo CD, Flux) pulls and syncs the cluster, so changes and rollbacks are commits.
mistakes: kubectl edits in production bypassing Git.

q: Name common Dockerfile instructions.
short: FROM (base), RUN (build commands), COPY/ADD (files), WORKDIR, ENV, EXPOSE, CMD/ENTRYPOINT (startup), USER, VOLUME, LABEL.

q: Write a Dockerfile for a FastAPI model service with fast rebuilds.
short: FROM python:3.x-slim; WORKDIR /app; COPY requirements.txt; RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt; COPY model and code; EXPOSE 8000; CMD uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000.

q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
short: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments or a default command that docker run arguments override. Combined: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] CMD ["serve.py"].
example: docker run img train.py overrides CMD.

q: A pod keeps restarting (CrashLoopBackOff). How do you debug?
short: kubectl describe pod (events, exit codes), kubectl logs --previous, check image tag and command, env/config and secrets, resource limits (OOMKilled), liveness probe timing (model loading slower than probe).
example: Probe kills pod before 40 s model load.

q: How does the Kubernetes scheduler choose a node?
short: Filters nodes that satisfy resource requests, constraints, taints/tolerations and affinity, then scores them (e.g. spreading load, preferring less-utilised nodes) and binds the pod to the best.

q: How do rolling updates work, and how do you roll back?
short: The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods gradually (maxSurge/maxUnavailable) while readiness probes gate traffic; kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet (or revert the Git commit under GitOps).

q: Design CI/CD for an ML model service.
short: On PR: lint, unit/data tests, small training smoke test. On merge: build and scan image, push with immutable tag, update deployment repo; Argo CD syncs staging; run integration and shadow tests; promote to production via a reviewed commit; monitor and roll back by revert.
mistakes: Training inside the CI build of the serving image.

q: What is a Kubernetes Service and why is it needed?
short: A stable virtual IP/DNS name and load balancer in front of a set of pods selected by labels; pods are ephemeral with changing IPs, so clients need a stable endpoint.

q: Should model weights be inside the image?
short: Small models: baking in gives immutable, reproducible images. Large or frequently updated models: download from a registry or object store at start-up (or mount a volume), keeping images small, but version and verify them.

q: Autoscale a GPU inference service on Kubernetes.
short: Request GPUs as resources; use HPA on custom metrics (queue length, GPU utilisation, request latency) rather than CPU; cluster autoscaler adds GPU nodes; warm pools to hide model-load time; batching to maximise GPU use.
detail: CPU metrics mislead for GPU work.
mistakes: Scaling on CPU for GPU-bound pods.

q: How do you secure ML containers?
short: Minimal base images, pinned versions and digests, vulnerability scanning, non-root USER, read-only filesystems, secrets from a secret store (not ENV in images), signed images, network policies, least-privilege service accounts.

q: Push-based vs pull-based (GitOps) deployment?
short: Push: CI has cluster credentials and runs kubectl/helm; simple but credentials spread and drift is undetected. Pull: an in-cluster agent syncs from Git, detects and corrects drift, keeps credentials inside the cluster, and makes history auditable.
mistakes: Storing plain secrets in the deploy repo.

q: Why do containers start faster than VMs, technically?
short: A container is an isolated process using kernel namespaces and cgroups on the already-running host kernel, so there's no OS boot; a VM must boot a full guest kernel and OS on virtualised hardware.
follow: Security implications of a shared kernel?

q: Your model image is 9 GB and deploys slowly. Fix it.
short: Use slim/distroless bases, multi-stage builds to drop compilers, install only runtime dependencies (CPU vs GPU wheels), remove caches, move large weights to a volume or object store, and order layers for caching.
mistakes: Installing the full CUDA toolkit for CPU inference.

q: How does Kubernetes self-heal and what are its limits?
short: kubelet restarts failed containers; controllers recreate missing pods; the scheduler moves pods off failed nodes; services route only to ready pods. Limits: it can't fix bad code, data or config, insufficient capacity leaves pods Pending, and stateful workloads need extra care.
example: Pending pods when the cluster is full.
mistakes: Assuming restarts fix a crash bug.
